d: A 32-bit number that encodes what a property is, not just which one it is.
x: A property ID packs four things into one number: which namespace it belongs to (Google's or a vendor's), what part of the car it applies to, what data type it holds, and a unique identifier. Reading the number tells you a lot before you loo

d: Which specific seat, door or window a value applies to.
x: Many properties exist several times over — one per seat, per door, per window. The area ID says which one. Crucially it is a set of flags, not a counter: the driver's seat is 0x0001 and the front passenger's is 0x0004, not 1 and 2.

d: The namespace car makers use for properties Google has not defined.

d: The class an Android app uses to read and write vehicle values.
x: CarPropertyManager is the app-facing API for vehicle data. An app asks it for a property value or subscribes to changes; it forwards the request to Car Service, which checks permissions and asks the VHAL.

d: The shared wire that ECUs use to broadcast short messages to each other.
x: CAN is the most common vehicle network. ECUs broadcast small numbered messages; anything interested listens. It is fast, extremely reliable and decades old, and it carries no notion of "requests" — just a continuous stream of announcements.

d: The wiring and protocols the car's computers use to talk to each other.
x: Collectively the CAN, LIN, FlexRay and Automotive Ethernet links inside a vehicle. Android does not connect to these directly — a vendor component does, and translates for the VHAL.

d: Whether a value is fixed, announced when it moves, or sampled continuously.
x: STATIC means it never changes after startup, like the VIN. ON_CHANGE means the VHAL announces it whenever it moves, like gear position. CONTINUOUS means it is sampled at a rate, like speed. Choosing wrong either wastes power or makes the UI

d: Asking to be told whenever a value changes, instead of repeatedly asking for it.
x: An app registers a callback for a property, and the platform delivers updates. This is always preferable to polling: it wakes fewer components and uses far less power.

d: The part of Android that owns everything car-related.
x: Car Service is a single system process holding a dozen smaller services: vehicle properties, audio zones, power state, user switching, driver distraction, watchdog. Apps reach the vehicle through it, and it checks permissions on the way.

d: The library apps use to reach car features, the way android.media is used for audio.
x: android.car is the public API surface for automotive. It contains CarPropertyManager, CarAudioManager, CarUxRestrictionsManager and others. Apps link against it; it talks to Car Service behind the scenes.

d: The single Android process that hosts most of the operating system's services.
x: system_server runs the window manager, activity manager, package manager and dozens more. It is the most important process on the device — if it crashes, the whole user interface restarts.

d: How one Android process asks another process to do something.
x: Binder is Android's mechanism for communication between processes. An app calling CarPropertyManager is really sending a Binder message to Car Service. It is fast, but not free — and each process has a limited pool of threads to handle inco

d: A small language for describing what one process is allowed to ask another.
x: You write an .aidl file listing methods and their arguments; the build generates the code that packs them into Binder messages. It is how HALs and system services publish their interfaces.

d: The older version of AIDL, used for HALs before Android 13.
x: HIDL served the same purpose as AIDL for hardware interfaces. AOSP has moved HAL interfaces to AIDL; HIDL remains in older vehicles and is gradually being retired.

d: An invisible account that runs the car's software before anyone logs in.
x: On a phone, user 0 is you. In a car, user 0 has no screen at all — it exists to run climate, audio and the vehicle connection so the car works with nobody signed in. Drivers are separate users layered on top, and switching between them neve

d: A seat position, together with the screens and the user that belong to it.
x: A cockpit may have a driver display, a cluster, a passenger screen and rear screens, with different people using them at once. Occupant zones model who is sitting where, which screens they own, and which user account is theirs.

d: A service that checks other processes are still responding, and kills the ones that are not.
x: CarWatchdog pings registered services and terminates any that stop answering. It also tracks how much each app writes to storage, because vehicle flash memory has to survive fifteen years.

d: The permanent bars and panels around the edge of the screen.
x: CarSystemUI draws the status bar, the navigation bar, the climate panel and the notification surface. Your app only ever gets the region between them, and the bars stay on top at all times.

d: A separate app that replaces another app's colours, sizes and layouts without changing its code.

d: Rules the platform enforces on what your screen may show while the car is moving.
x: Above a speed threshold, the platform limits how many list items you may display, how long your text may be, whether video may play and whether a keyboard may appear. These are enforced by Android itself, not left to each app to honour.

d: A flag an app sets to claim a screen is safe to show while driving.
x: An activity marked distractionOptimized may be displayed while the vehicle is moving. Without it, the platform replaces the screen with a "not available while driving" message. Setting it is a safety claim that a car maker will test.

d: The fast path that puts the reversing camera on screen before Android has finished starting.
x: Regulations in many markets require a reversing image within about two seconds. Android takes far longer to boot, so the camera path deliberately bypasses the Android framework and runs as a small native service that can start almost immedi

d: The screen behind the steering wheel showing speed and warning lamps.
x: The instrument cluster displays legally required information. On many vehicles it is not driven by Android at all but by a separate certified system, with Android sending it content to display in one designated area.

d: A warning lamp — seatbelt, airbag, engine — on the instrument cluster.
x: Telltales have legal requirements for colour, symbol and availability. They are almost never drawn by Android, because a general-purpose operating system cannot guarantee they will appear.

d: A place in the car with its own volume and its own idea of what is playing.
x: The cabin is usually zone 0. A rear-seat entertainment system can be zone 1, with its own volume control and its own audio focus, so a passenger's film does not pause when the driver gets a navigation prompt.

d: What kind of sound this is — music, navigation, phone call, warning chime.
x: The audio context is derived from what an app says its sound is for. It decides which speakers the sound reaches and what happens to it when something more important starts playing.

x: A car head unit exposes several separate outputs rather than one. Music goes out one, navigation another. Keeping them separate lets the amplifier lower the music behind a navigation prompt in hardware, without any software involvement.

d: The system deciding who is allowed to make noise right now.
x: When two things want to play, focus decides the outcome: one stops, one pauses, or both play with one quieter. In a car some sounds — collision warnings — cannot be interrupted at all, so requests that would interrupt them are simply refuse

x: When a navigation prompt plays, the music does not stop — it gets quieter for a moment. That is ducking. It can be done by the app, by Android, or by the amplifier in hardware.

d: The choice of which device and which build flavour you are compiling.
x: Before building AOSP you run `lunch` and pick a target, such as a car emulator in debug configuration. It determines which code is compiled, which apps are included and what the resulting image runs on.

d: The file listing what software goes into a particular device's image.
x: A product makefile names the apps, HALs, configuration files and settings that make up one device. Board configuration, separately, describes the hardware it runs on.

d: The build system AOSP uses, configured with Android.bp files.
x: Soong reads declarative Android.bp files describing each module — its sources, its dependencies, which partition it belongs on — and works out how to build everything. It replaced the older Make-based system.

x: Over-the-air updates let a car maker fix software after a vehicle is sold. Because there is no way to recover a vehicle that fails mid-update, the design writes the new version to a spare copy of the storage and switches over only once it i

d: Two complete copies of the system, so an update can be written while the car runs on the other.
x: The vehicle runs from slot A while the update is written to slot B. A reboot switches to B. If B fails to start, the bootloader falls back to A automatically. There is never a moment where the car has neither a working system nor a spare.

d: A window after the car is switched off when it may still do background work.
x: The engine is off and the driver has gone, but the head unit stays awake briefly to apply updates, upload diagnostics and sync data — work nobody should have to wait for while driving. The window is limited, so tasks must be able to stop pa

d: What the head unit is doing when the car is not being driven.
x: A head unit is rarely fully off. It suspends, so it can wake in about a second when the driver returns. The power state machine covers booting, running, preparing to shut down, and the different depths of sleep.

d: How long from switching the car on to the software being usable.
x: Car makers commit to specific figures, and some are legal requirements — a reversing camera image within roughly two seconds. Boot time is measured on real hardware from the ignition signal, not from when Android starts.

d: A permission system in the Linux kernel that says which programs may touch which files.
x: SELinux labels every process and every file, and a policy lists what is allowed. Anything not explicitly permitted is denied. On Android it is always on, and it is the usual reason a correctly written program silently does nothing.

d: A log line saying SELinux blocked something.
x: When SELinux refuses an operation it logs a denial naming who tried, what they touched and what they wanted to do. Denials do not usually crash anything — the operation simply fails — which is why a value that is wrong but consistent is so

d: The rule that hardware code and Android code are kept separate and talk only through fixed interfaces.
x: Treble splits the system into partitions: Android framework on one, hardware-specific code on another. They communicate only through versioned, stable interfaces. This is what allows Android to be upgraded on a vehicle years later without e

d: A manifest listing which hardware interfaces a device provides, and at which version.
x: The Vendor Interface Object declares each HAL a device implements. Android checks it at startup, and apps can ask whether an interface exists — which is how a feature can be absent on a cheaper trim without anything crashing.

d: A permission only apps built into the car's software can hold.
x: Reading the speed is an ordinary permission any app can request. Moving a window is not — that requires the app to be part of the vehicle image and signed with the car maker's key. This is a schedule decision as much as a technical one: suc

d: Each stage of startup checking the next is genuine before running it.
x: A key burned into the chip verifies the bootloader, which verifies the system, and so on. If any stage has been tampered with, the vehicle refuses to start it. This is why the software cannot simply be edited on a production car.

d: A rating for how dangerous it is if a particular function fails.
x: ASIL levels run from A to D, D being the most critical. The rating decides how rigorously something must be developed and tested. Android is generally not rated at all, which is why anything safety-critical — telltales, airbag control — run

d: Google's automated tests that check a device behaves like Android is supposed to.
x: CTS runs thousands of tests against the framework. Passing is required to ship with Google services, and failures usually mean a car maker changed platform behaviour that apps rely on.

d: Tests that check the hardware-facing code honours its interfaces.
x: Where CTS tests the framework, VTS tests HALs. For the VHAL it checks the property list is well formed, areas are consistent, and declared limits are actually enforced.

d: An industry-standard naming scheme for car data, like Vehicle.Speed.
x: The Vehicle Signal Specification is a shared tree of signal names, types and units maintained by an industry body. Its value is that a supplier, a platform team and a UI team can agree on one definition instead of each keeping a private lis

d: The software standard most car ECUs are built to.
x: AUTOSAR defines how automotive control software is structured. Its signal definitions are published in an XML format called ARXML, which is usually the original source of truth for what data a vehicle produces.

d: A way for car components to offer services to each other over a network, rather than just broadcasting.
x: Where CAN broadcasts numbered messages, SOME/IP lets a component publish named services that others discover and call. It is part of the shift from wiring signals together to treating vehicle functions as software services.

d: Designing a car so its features come from software that can be changed later.
x: A software-defined vehicle treats functions as software running on general-purpose computers, rather than fixed behaviour wired into dedicated ECUs. In practice it means fewer, more powerful computers, service-based communication, and featu

d: Software that runs several separate operating systems on one chip, keeping them isolated.
x: A modern cockpit computer may run Android for infotainment and a safety-rated system for the instrument cluster on the same silicon. The hypervisor partitions the hardware so a fault in one cannot affect the other.

d: Positioning from satellites — GPS is one system among several.
x: Global Navigation Satellite System is the umbrella term for GPS (US), Galileo (EU), GLONASS (Russia) and BeiDou (China). A modern receiver uses several at once, which is why position is far better than GPS alone used to be.

d: Working out where you are from how fast and which way you have been going, when satellites are unavailable.
x: In a tunnel or a multi-storey car park there is no satellite signal. Dead reckoning keeps estimating position from wheel rotation, steering angle and gyroscope data until the signal returns. Error accumulates the longer it runs.

d: A count of how far each wheel has rotated, used to measure distance precisely.
x: Wheel speed sensors produce pulses as the wheel turns. Counting them gives a far more accurate distance measurement than integrating speed, which is why they feed dead reckoning and odometry.

d: The systems that help or intervene while driving — lane keeping, adaptive cruise, emergency braking.
x: ADAS covers everything from a lane departure warning to automatic emergency braking. It runs on its own dedicated, safety-rated hardware; Android generally only receives its state to display, and never controls it.

d: A camera watching the driver to detect drowsiness or distraction.
x: A driver monitoring system uses an infrared camera pointed at the driver to estimate gaze direction and eye closure. In several markets it is becoming a regulatory requirement. The camera feed is highly sensitive personal data and normally

x: Standardised by the Car Connectivity Consortium. It uses secure hardware on both the phone and the vehicle, with ultra-wideband or Bluetooth for proximity. Android is usually not in the trust path at all — a dedicated secure module handles

d: A file Android writes when a native program crashes, recording exactly where.
x: When C or C++ code crashes, the system captures the registers, the stack and the memory map into a tombstone file under /data/tombstones. With the matching symbols it can be turned back into readable function names.

d: Android deciding an app has stopped responding to input and offering to close it.
x: If an app does not handle input within a few seconds, or a service does not start in time, Android declares an ANR. On a vehicle these are more serious than on a phone: the driver cannot pull over to deal with a frozen screen.

d: A description of what hardware exists, handed to the kernel at boot.
x: Rather than compiling hardware details into the kernel, a device tree describes the board: which chips are on which bus, which pins do what, which display is attached. The same kernel can then boot different boards.

d: A small battery-backed clock that keeps time while the car is off.
x: The real-time clock runs on its own tiny power supply so the vehicle knows roughly what time it is at startup, before any network or satellite fix. It drifts, which is why the time is corrected once a better source is available.

d: How full the high-voltage battery is, as a percentage.
x: The equivalent of a fuel gauge for an electric vehicle. It is an estimate rather than a direct measurement, computed by the battery management system from voltage, current and temperature.

d: A phone drawing a car interface and sending the picture to the head unit.
x: Android Auto and Apple CarPlay both work this way. Confusingly, an AAOS vehicle can also host projection — the car runs Android as its own operating system AND can display a projected phone session as one more app.

d: Grouping the wiring by where things are in the car, rather than by what they do.
x: Instead of a lighting ECU wired to every lamp in the vehicle, a zonal design puts a small controller in each corner of the car. It connects to whatever is physically near it and links back to a central computer over one high-speed cable. Wi

d: One powerful computer running many vehicle functions that used to have their own boxes.
x: Rather than a hundred small controllers, a few capable processors run the software for many functions at once. This is what makes a function updatable, replaceable and addable after the vehicle ships.

d: A publish-subscribe messaging standard used where large amounts of data must move with predictable timing.
x: Where SOME/IP suits request-response service calls, DDS suits continuous high-volume streams with quality-of-service guarantees — which is why it appears in ADAS and robotics rather than body electronics.

d: Extensions that make ordinary Ethernet deliver messages on a guaranteed schedule.
x: Standard Ethernet is fast but makes no promise about when a packet arrives. Time-Sensitive Networking adds scheduling and reservation so a control message cannot be delayed by a video stream — which is what a vehicle needs before it can rep

d: Components offer named capabilities that others discover and call, instead of broadcasting values.
x: A seat controller offers a SeatService with a setPosition method; anything that needs it discovers the service at runtime and calls it. Adding a new consumer requires no network redesign, which is the property that lets features be added af

d: A software copy of a vehicle computer, running on a normal machine with no hardware involved.
x: A virtual ECU lets the real production software be tested on a laptop or a build server. It is the foundation of shift-left testing: defects that would otherwise need a physical vehicle can be found in a pipeline run.

d: A simulated model of a specific vehicle, kept in step with the real one.
x: A digital twin mirrors a real vehicle's configuration and state closely enough to reproduce its behaviour. It is used to test an update against what a customer actually has, rather than against a generic reference build.

d: A capability already present in the vehicle, unlocked after purchase.
x: The hardware and software shipped with the car; buying the feature issues a signed entitlement the vehicle verifies locally. Commercially attractive and reputationally sensitive — customers object to paying for hardware they already own.

d: The version of AUTOSAR built for powerful processors and service-based communication.
x: Classic AUTOSAR targets small microcontrollers with fixed scheduling. Adaptive targets microprocessors running POSIX operating systems, with dynamic scheduling and SOME/IP services. Both exist in the same vehicle, doing different jobs.

d: Finding defects earlier, where they are cheaper to fix.
x: Moving testing from late stages that need physical vehicles to early stages that run in a build pipeline. In vehicle software the cost difference between the two is enormous — minutes versus a scheduled test slot.

d: A guarantee that one part of a system cannot disturb a more safety-critical part.
x: When a safety-rated function shares hardware with an unrated one, functional safety standards require proof that the unrated one cannot affect it — through memory, timing or shared resources. It is the requirement that hypervisor partitioni

x: Traditionally anything on the vehicle network was trusted implicitly. Zero trust replaces that with authentication and authorisation between components, so a compromised part cannot simply command the others.

d: A build system that produces a custom Linux distribution from recipes.
x: Rather than shipping a distribution, Yocto builds one to your specification — you choose every package that goes in. In automotive this matters because you must account for every binary on the device for security and licence compliance, and

d: A test bench where real ECU hardware runs against a simulated vehicle.

x: R155 covers cybersecurity management, R156 covers software update management. They are type-approval requirements in the EU, UK, Japan, Korea and elsewhere — without them a vehicle cannot legally be sold. They turned security and update pro
